intervention.description: finalization of sample preparation on a water-cooled Cu hearth

structure.description: composed of the fcc and hexagonal C14 phases

evidence_spans: The as-cast polycrystalline sample (1.5 g) of FeCoNiTi was prepared through a homemade arc furnace.

The elemental components, Fe chips (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory, 99.9%), Co chips (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory, 99.9%), Ni wire (Soekawa Rikagaku, 99.9%), and Ti wire (Nilaco, 99.9%), were employed in a fixed atomic ratio of Fe:Co:Ni:Ti = 1:1:1:1.
These constituent elements were remelted several times on a water-cooled Cu hearth and flipped each time to ensure homogeneity under Ar atmosphere.
The finalization of the sample preparation involved rapid quenching on the water-cooled Cu hearth.
As mentioned in the next section, the as-cast FeCoNiTi is composed of the fcc and hexagonal C14 phases with the volume ratio of V fcc : V C14 = 57:43.
Chemical composition analysis indicates that the fcc phase is Fe 21.3 Co 24.8 Ni 32.2 Ti 21.6 , while the C14 phase is Fe 27.3 Co 26.6 Ni 17.4 Ti 28.7 .
Both phases undergo ferromagnetic (FM) ordering.

evidence_spans: To determine which phase is responsible for each ordering, we prepared as-cast Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 , corresponding to Fe 27.3 Co 26.6 Ni 17.4 Ti 28.7 of the C14 phase in FeCoNiTi, using an analogous procedure.
As anticipated, Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 is predominantly composed of the C14 phase.
Comparing the magnetic properties of FeCoNiTi and Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 elucidates which phase is responsible for the respective ordering temperatures.

material.name: FeCoNiTi
material.initial_state: dual-phase with fcc (57 vol%) and C14 (43 vol%)

intervention.description: Measured temperature dependence of dc susceptibility χdc under external field

structure.description: Dual-phase structure with fcc and C14 Laves phases

evidence_units.mechanism: FM orderings in both fcc and C14 phases contribute to magnetic response, with fcc phase exhibiting two distinct ordering temperatures
evidence_spans: Figure 2 a illustrates χ dc ( T ) under an external field H of 100 Oe for FeCoNiTi, employing a logarithmic scale for χ dc .
As the temperature decreases from 1150 K, χ dc sharply rises around 1100 K, followed by a plateau extending to approximately 300 K. Subsequent cooling prompts a second notable increase in χ dc .
These outcomes suggest the presence of at least two FM phases in FeCoNiTi, a phenomenon explicable by FM orderings in both the fcc and C14 phases.
To ascertain the Curie temperature ( T c ), the temperature derivative of χ dc is depicted in Figure 2 a.
The local minima of d χ dc / dT define the T c values, a methodology widely applied in analyzing transition metal-based alloys and compounds.
The thus-obtained T c values are 1084, 214, and 168 K.

The subsequent discussion delves into assigning two phases to their respective ordering temperatures. The comparison of χ dc ( T ) between FeCoNiTi and C14 phase dominant Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 suggests that the FM orderings at T c = 1084 and 168 K occur in the fcc phase and that at T c = 214 K is induced by the C14 phase

evidence_units.mechanism: Negative correlation between coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms) governed by magnetocrystalline anisotropy in fcc phase

comparison.direction: Hc reaches 489 and 667 Oe at 300 and 400 K, respectively

evidence_spans: To evaluate the magnetic contribution solely from the fcc phase, M – H curves originating from the fcc phase are extracted through the following procedure.

For FeCoNiTi, comprising fcc (57% vol.) and C14 (43% vol.) phases, the weight fraction ratio is determined as fcc:C14 = 59:41, leveraging density values of 7.8241 g/cm 3 for fcc and 7.2632 g/cm 3 for C14.

Subsequently, assuming that the H dependence of M ( M ( H )) of the C14 phase mirrors that of Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 , M ( H ) of the fcc phase at a fixed temperature can be computed using the equation: 1 where M ( H ) FeCoNiTi and M ( H ) Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 represent the magnetization of FeCoNiTi and Fe 27 Co 27 Ni 17 Ti 29 , as illustrated in Figures 2 b and 3 b, respectively.
The deduced M ( H ) of the fcc phase is exhibited in Figure 3 c.

At 300 and 400 K, H c reaches 489 and 667 Oe, respectively (refer to the inset of Figure 3 c), categorizing the fcc Fe 21 Co 25 Ni 32 Ti 22 above 300 K as high H c materials within the realm of fcc HEAs based on FeCoNi.
Within the fcc Fe 21 Co 25 Ni 32 Ti 22 , the decrease in temperature leads to a reduction in H c and concurrent augmentation of high-field magnetization, as depicted in Figure 3 c.
This observation implies a negative correlation between H c and M s .

material.name: fcc phase
material.initial_state: cubic structure with space group No. 225

intervention.description: Electronic structure calculations to determine density of states and magnetic moments

structure.description: fcc phase with FM ground state

evidence_units.mechanism: Disparate energy dependence of total DOS between spin-up and spin-down at Fermi energy (EF) substantiates FM ground state
evidence_spans: Electronic structure calculations were executed to elucidate the ferromagnetic characteristics inherent in each phase, and the outcomes are delineated in Figure 4 a–f.
Figure 4 a,b presents the total density of states (DOS) and partial DOSs specifically for the fcc phase.
The chemical composition of the fcc phase is denoted by Fe 21 Co 25 Ni 32 Ti 22 , as determined by EDX analysis, and the experimental lattice parameter is employed.
The disparate energy dependence of total DOS between spin-up and spin-down at E F substantiates the FM ground state in the fcc phase.
This signifies that the magnetic moment is the largest for the Fe atom and the smallest for the Ni atom, as listed in Table 1 . Notably, these atoms exhibit FM coupling to each other.
Table 1 compares spin moments for the constituent elements in the fcc phase with their counterparts in the C14 phase.
In both phases, the magnetic moments of Fe, Co, and Ni exhibit ferromagnetic alignment, while the orientation of the Ti moment is antiparallel to that of Fe, Co, or Ni.
Notably, within each elemental category, the absolute magnitude of the magnetic moment in the fcc phase exceeds that obtained in the C14 phase.

evidence_units.mechanism: Electronic structure calculation lends credence to existence of low-temperature FM ordering
evidence_spans: Subsequently, we assessed M s and compared it with the experimental counterpart in each phase.
In the fcc phase, the theoretical M s is ascertained to be 78.6 emu/g, employing the identical equation ( eq 2 ), with the molecular weight of the fcc phase being 55.77 g.

As depicted in Figure 3 c, the high-field M at 300 K is 10.8 emu/g, markedly smaller than the anticipated theoretical M s . Upon cooling to 50 K, the high-field M escalates to 43 emu/g, leading to a notable diminution in the disparity between experimental and theoretical values.

Given that theoretical values are typically acquired at 0 K, the electronic structure calculation lends credence to the existence of low-temperature FM ordering in addition to the high-temperature counterpart at 1084 K.
